input: This memo considers whether the plant should invest in sensors for the early detection of bearing deterioration, and it recommends that, rather than proceeding immediately to a full installation, the plant should first undertake a three-month pilot so that the benefits can be demonstrated on our own equipment before a major commitment is made. The reliability engineering group would own the pilot and would report in good time for the March capital review, at which point the decision on full installation can properly be taken. There are 214 pumps running at the plant, and the maintenance records for the last 12 months show a total of 1328 h of unplanned downtime, a very considerable figure, of which bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours, making bearings by far the single largest identified contributor. A sensor set covering all 214 pumps has been quoted at $450k installed, plus a further $59k per year in ongoing costs, so the financial commitment involved in going straight to full installation is by no means trivial. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors succeeded in cutting downtime by 27%, which is an encouraging result, although it must be acknowledged that this figure comes from the vendor and was not measured here at this plant, on our own machines, under our own operating conditions. The proposed pilot would equip 22 pumps at a cost of $36k over three months, and it would show whether a downtime reduction of that order is achievable in our service before the larger sum is committed. It should also be noted that spare-part lead times are entirely unaffected by the sensors, so no benefit on that side should be anticipated. In summary, the recommendation is to proceed with the pilot and to hold the decision on full installation until the pilot results are reported.
target: The reliability engineering group recommends a three-month pilot of bearing sensors on 22 pumps, at $36k, before any decision on plant-wide installation. The group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported. The evidence base is the plant maintenance record for 12 months. The plant runs 214 pumps, and the record shows 1328 h of unplanned downtime, of which bearing failures account for 39% of the hours. Full installation is quoted at $450k installed for all 214 pumps, plus $59k per year. Against that cost stands one performance figure: in a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 27%. The figure is a vendor figure, measured on another plant's equipment, and it is not evidence for this plant. The trade-off the pilot resolves is the pilot cost spent now against the full installation price committed on an unverified figure. The pilot measures the downtime reduction in this service, on the bearings that produce the largest share of the downtime hours, and returns a plant figure in place of the vendor figure. One limit stands regardless of the outcome: spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, and no benefit is claimed on that side. If the pilot returns a reduction well below the vendor figure, the full installation case is rebuilt on the pilot number or not brought forward at all.
